title: Why is it called a 'cockpit'? | AVIATION WORDS

entries.note: Means 'birdiness', from Latin [[from:avis]], bird; coined in 1863 by [[see:Gabriel de La Landelle]] on the model of [[from:navigation]].
Jess calls it 'oceaniness'; the model on which [[gave:aviation]] was coined.
First recorded in an 1887 translation of [[see:Jules Verne]]'s [[see:Clipper of the Clouds]], which also coins [[see:aviating]].
Coined in the same 1887 translation of [[see:Clipper of the Clouds]] as [[see:aviator]], but never adopted in English.
French writer whose works gave English [[see:aviator]]; he helped popularise [[see:helicopter]] after learning of [[see:Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt]]'s inventions.
Novel by [[see:Jules Verne]], inspired by the spiralifer inventions, whose 1887 translation gives the first [[see:aviator]]; its flying machine is the [[see:Albatross]].
Coined [[see:aviation]] in 1863 and invented [[see:spiralifer]]s with his friend [[see:Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt]].
American form, a deliberate alteration of [[from:aeroplane]], which also ended up in American publications; the RAF and the BBC once pushed it in Britain without success.
British form from French, which [[gave:airplane]]; it refers to the flat, now curved, lifting surface and first meant a flat-surfaced airship.
Early mispronunciation of [[see:aeroplane]], which Jess calls a metathesis, cited as a reason for the American change to [[see:airplane]].
Keeps the aero- that Americans dropped from [[see:airplane]], like [[see:aerospace]].
Keeps the aero- of [[see:aeroplane]] in the more scientific vocabulary of flight.
Britain took up this altered form rather than aeroport, unlike its loyalty to [[see:aeroplane]].
Rob's favourite plane, which he has never flown in: a feat of engineering that floats like a butterfly but looks like a whale.
Jess's favourite: a small British single-seat biplane and a cuter version of the [[see:Sopwith Camel]].
Well-known fighter that Snoopy pretends his doghouse is, compared with the [[see:Sopwith Pup]].
Rob thinks he should have picked it as his favourite because it carried Rolls-Royce Merlin engines, made in his hometown.
Big employer in Rob's hometown that supplied his school with stationery printed with [[see:suck, squeeze, bang, blow]].
Cheeky unofficial slogan of the jet engine industry describing how a [[see:jet]] works, printed on rulers given to Rob's school by [[see:Rolls-Royce]].
From French [[from:jeter]], to throw, because a jet throws out liquid or gas to push forward; from the same root as [[same-root:ejaculate]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:jet]], to Rob's embarrassment.
Aviation slang discussed in an earlier episode, an example of the lewd humour in aviation.
Book that revealed the machismo of the early American aviation and space programmes.
Like [[see:aeroplane]], it refers to a surface shape rather than a vehicle.
Unlike a [[see:hydroplane]], an actual vehicle; Jess sees them flying over the lakes near her home.
The big saltwater lakes or lagoons of southern France, from which water-scooping planes collect water to fight forest fires.
One of the -naut words that show aviation vocabulary borrowed from sailing, like [[see:astronaut]] and [[see:cosmonaut]].
A -naut word showing flight vocabulary borrowed from seafaring, like [[see:aeronaut]].
A -naut word showing flight vocabulary borrowed from seafaring, like [[see:aeronaut]].
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
One of the parts of a plane named after parts of a ship.
First a pit for cockfighting; 17th-century sailors used it for the cramped coxswain's station near the stern, and early 20th-century, WWI-era aviation took it up for the pilot's area.

Middle French, first a shelter for ships or large equipment, from Germanic elements like [[same-root:home]] and [[same-root:yard]] by way of Middle Dutch; Jess thinks a claimed French verb origin is bogus.
Shares a Germanic element with [[same-root:hangar]].
Shares a Germanic element with [[same-root:hangar]].
French technical term for the tail section, meaning 'the feathering' after the end of an arrow; related to [[same-root:pen]] and [[same-root:penne]].
From the same word as [[same-root:empennage]]; like [[see:quill]], it meant a feather before a writing tool.
Same meaning as [[see:pen]]: a feather first, then something to write with.
Pasta named because it is shaped like little quills, so it is related to [[same-root:empennage]].
French word meaning spindle-shaped, related to [[same-root:fusilli]], [[same-root:fusée]] and [[same-root:fusil]].
Spindle-shaped pasta related to [[same-root:fuselage]]; Jess wants to build a plane from pasta.
French for a rocket, which basically means a spindle; from the same source as [[same-root:fuselage]].
Another spindle-shaped French word from the same source as [[same-root:fuselage]].
French word for the movable parts that make a plane bank, literally 'little wings'.
The parts that change the wing's shape and surface area, and so its lift, mentioned alongside [[see:aileron]]s.
From Latin [[from:ala]], wing; its S came from confusion with [[see:isle]] and the A from French [[see:aile]]; first the side wings of churches.
Its spelling was taken up by [[see:aisle]], which has no etymological S.
French for a wing, which the added A makes [[see:aisle]] look more like.
The central part of a church, separated from the [[see:aisle]]s by rows of pillars.
Said of an engine that died mid-flight, and of tired people; from a ship that 'pooped', meaning it was hit by a wave over the [[from:poop]].
A ship's highest deck, formed by the roof of the stern cabin, which [[gave:pooped out]].
Aviation term from around WWII: ball-shaped throttle and joystick grips were pushed forward toward the [[see:firewall]] for maximum power or a dive.
The fire-resistant bulkhead between the engine and the pilot, the wall of [[see:balls to the wall]].

entries.term: flying by the seat of your pants
entries.note: From flying without instruments, on feel and instinct, sensing the plane's vibrations through the seat of your pants.
An intense, tangled close-quarters fight in the air, named on the same model as [[see:cockpit]].
Confirms a message was received; from the phonetic alphabet, where R for 'received' was [[from:Roger]], now [[see:Romeo]].
Distress call from French for 'help me', chosen in the early 1920s by [[see:Frederick Stanley Mockford]] because both English and French speakers could say it.
Officer in charge of radio at [[see:Croydon Airport]] who coined [[see:Mayday]], since much air traffic ran between Croydon and Paris.
The big early airport, often forgotten because Croydon is now a nondescript part of south-east England not far from Heathrow.
Paris airport at the other end of much early traffic from [[see:Croydon Airport]], which shaped the choice of [[see:Mayday]].
From a training aircraft of around 1909 to the 1910s called the taxi, used on the ground, because hopping in and out felt like a taxi ride.
Used in 1930s aviation for trainees following leaders through ever-tighter manoeuvres, then any competitive daily grind; it also referred to actual rat racing.
Greek helico-, spiral, plus pter-, wing, wrongly rebracketed as -copter; coined by [[see:Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt]] and popularised by [[see:Jules Verne]].
[[see:helicopter]] is Jess's best surprising example, mistakenly split to give -copter words like [[see:gyrocopter]].
Formed from the mistaken -copter split of [[see:helicopter]].
Means 'finger wing', sharing pter- with [[same-root:helicopter]]; its P is silent only because English phonotactics forbid starting a word with pt-.
Coin expert and inventor who coined [[see:helicopter]] and invented [[see:spiralifer]]s with [[see:Gabriel de La Landelle]].
Mini helicopters named for their spiraliferous propellers, invented by [[see:Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt]] and [[see:Gabriel de La Landelle]].
English phonotactics forbid an initial pt-, which is why the P of [[see:pterodactyl]] is silent.
The flying machine in [[see:Clipper of the Clouds]], a multi-rotor gyrodyne or compound helicopter lifted by vertical air screws.
Named after [[from:Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin]], who supposedly perfected the airship; short for German [[from:Zeppelin-Luftschiff]].
Airship whose sad disaster is part of German and American history, hardly evidence that the [[see:Zeppelin]] was perfected.
Supposed perfecter of the airship, which is named [[see:Zeppelin]] after him.
The original German name for the airship, which [[gave:Zeppelin]].
From French [[from:diriger]], to direct, related to [[same-root:direct]]: a steerable airship, unlike a balloon; Jess once punningly called a project dirigible.
Directly related to [[same-root:dirigible]].
A hot-air balloon, named after the [[from:Montgolfier brothers]] who invented it; unlike a [[see:dirigible]], it cannot be steered.
Inventors of the hot-air balloon, which is named [[see:montgolfière]] after them.
One theory, which the hosts doubt, says the prototype was nicknamed 'type B limp', without a framework, unlike the type A rigid.
Violent disturbance, from a Latin root for crowd or confusion that also gave [[same-root:disturb]], [[same-root:perturb]], [[same-root:turbo]] and [[same-root:turbine]].
From the same Latin root as [[same-root:turbulence]], making turbulence hard to define without its relatives.
From the same Latin root as [[same-root:turbulence]].
Draws on the rotational sense of the Latin root of [[same-root:turbulence]].
Draws on the rotational, stirring sense of the Latin root of [[same-root:turbulence]].
Originally nautical, from medieval Greek [[from:pēdōtēs]], a steering oar or helmsman, via Italian and French; related to words for feet, perhaps as the ship's foot.
Related to [[same-root:throat]]: throttling narrows a passage, as when throttling someone's throat.
The body part behind [[same-root:throttle]].
A crew member flying as a passenger to where they are needed; from theatre, where it meant a free, non-paying seat that filled the house.
The International Civil Aviation Organization, which made English aviation's official language and requires level four proficiency; its four-letter initialism is pronounced 'eye-kay-oh'.
Europe's busiest airport, full of French radio chatter; an Air France policy in 2000 to use English there lasted fifteen days.
Collision near New Delhi between a Saudi 747 and a Kazakh plane killing 349, partly blamed on English misunderstanding; [[see:ICAO]] cites it for its English rule.
The ICAO spelling alphabet, a century in the making, moving from place names to personal names; words were chosen to be pronounceable across languages.
Spelled with an F in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]] partly so Spanish speakers would not say 'alpa'.
Code word for B in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
Personal name used for C in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]] and the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]]; it replaced [[see:Coca]] late on.
D in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]], an exception to the vowel rule; replaced by [[see:Dixie]] at the [[see:Delta Air Lines]] hub.
Code word for E in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
Code word for F in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
Code word for G in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
Place name used for A in the earliest wave of spelling alphabets, before the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]].
Place name used for B in the earliest, place-name-based spelling alphabets.
Place name used for D in the earliest, place-name-based spelling alphabets.
Place name used for O in the earliest, place-name-based spelling alphabets.
Personal name used for B in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]], part of the shift to personal names.
R in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]], chosen over predecessors such as [[see:Robert]] and [[see:Roger]] whose vowels varied too much.
Predecessor of [[see:Romeo]] for R, in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet; it is Rob's name.
W in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet and the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]]; Jess's middle name.
A in the quaint WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet, which began 'apples, butter'.
B in the WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet, after [[see:Apples]].
P in the WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet.
Q in the WWI Royal Air Force spelling alphabet, which Rob finds very cute.
M in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet, paired with [[see:Nuts]] for N.
N in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet, after [[see:Monkey]] for M.
A cricket reference used for Y in the WWI Royal Air Force alphabet, now [[see:Yankee]].
Z in the RAF and [[see:Able Baker alphabet]]s, replaced by [[see:Zulu]] because it is pronounced differently in different places.
Current Z in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]], replacing [[see:Zebra]].
Current Y in the [[see:NATO phonetic alphabet]], replacing [[see:Yorker]].
Spelled with two Ts so French speakers would pronounce the final T.
The better-known American spelling alphabet of WWII, starting Able, [[see:Baker]], [[see:Charlie]]; Jess jokes it reads like a party shopping list.
A in the [[see:Able Baker alphabet]], which is named after it and [[see:Baker]].

Proposed in an ICAO South American variant; changed to [[see:Charlie]] very late in the NATO alphabet's development.
Code word in the alphabet proposed by the ICAO South American Regional Office.

One of the NATO words deliberately chosen as foreign words that also exist in English, like [[see:Tango]].
One of the NATO words deliberately chosen as foreign words that also exist in English, like [[see:Sierra]].
The very last change before the NATO alphabet was finalised, replacing [[see:Nectar]].
Former N, replaced by [[see:November]] because it could be confused with vector and sector and was hard for foreign speakers.
Former X, changed to [[see:X-ray]], so the word for X did not originally begin with X.
Former M, eventually changed to [[see:Mike]].
Former U, which became [[see:Uniform]].
Current U in the NATO alphabet, previously [[see:Union]].
The first X in the place-based alphabet, though it is Socrates's wife; unhelpful because it does not even start with the X sound.
Used for a taxiway D at the [[see:Delta Air Lines]] hub to avoid confusion with the airline; later dropped for its Confederate associations.
The airline whose hub airport used [[see:Dixie]] rather than [[see:Delta]] to avoid confusion.
Aviation pronunciation of three, one of the number forms meant to be understood over poor radio.
Aviation pronunciation of four, rhyming with 'lower' and spelled F-O-W-E-R on pronunciation charts.
Aviation pronunciation of five, because five sounds too much like 'fire', also why countdowns often skip five.
Aviation pronunciation of nine, perhaps because nine sounds like German [[see:nein]], or, as Rob suggests, like five.
German for no, which nine may sound too much like, one suggested reason for [[see:niner]].
International Telecommunication Union word for zero, used in some maritime circles, joining two ways of saying the number in one word.
ITU maritime word for one, combining two ways of saying the number, like [[see:nadazero]].
ITU maritime word for two, combining two ways of saying the number, like [[see:nadazero]].
ITU maritime word for three, combining two ways of saying the number, like [[see:nadazero]].
ITU maritime word for six, Rob's favourite, best said with a shimmy.
